text: Single pulses of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) applied concurrently with a visual target can either facilitate or impair detection performance, depending on factors such as stimulation intensity and brain state ( Silvanto et al., 2008 , 2017 ). Whereas TMS intensities above phosphene threshold have been found to mask visual perception when applied over the early visual cortex within a time window of 80–120 ms from stimulus onset (see e.g., Kammer et al., 2005 ; de Graaf et al., 2014 , for reviews), subthreshold TMS within the same time window can facilitate behavior (e.g., Abrahamyan et al., 2011 ), particularly when baseline performance is low, reflecting a situation with a weak perceptual signal (e.g., Schwarzkopf et al., 2011 ).
source_label: On the Mechanisms of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS): How Brain State and Baseline Performance Level Determine Behavioral Effects of TMS
